title: Around the World in Eighty Days
author: Jules Verne
wiki: Around the World in Eighty Days
ru: Англичанин Филеас Фогг заключает пари, что объедет весь мир за 80 дней, а за ним по пятам идёт сыщик.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Bet
chapters.text:
In 1872, at number 7 Savile Row in London, there lived a gentleman called Phileas Fogg. He was rich, but nobody knew where his money came from. He was polite, calm and very quiet. He never hurried, and he was never late.

Every day of his life was exactly the same. He got up at eight. At half past eleven he walked to the Reform Club — five hundred and seventy-six steps — and had breakfast there. He read the newspapers, played cards and ate dinner there. At midnight he went home to bed.

On the morning of 2 October, Mr Fogg had a problem. His servant brought him water for shaving at eighty-four degrees, not eighty-six. Two degrees too cold! So the servant lost his job.

At eleven o'clock a young Frenchman knocked at the door. He had a round, friendly face and strong arms.

“My name is Jean Passepartout,” he said. “It means 'goes everywhere'. I was a singer, a circus rider and a fireman. But now I want a quiet life, sir. People say you are the quietest man in England.”

Mr Fogg looked at his watch. “It is 11:29, Wednesday 2 October,” he said. “You are my servant from this minute.” Then he put on his hat and walked out.

On the wall of Passepartout's room hung a list of his jobs for every hour of the day. “Wonderful!” he thought. “My master is a machine. I'm going to be very happy here.”

That evening at the club, Mr Fogg's friends were talking about a famous crime. A few days before, a well-dressed thief took fifty-five thousand pounds from the Bank of England.

“He'll get away,” said Andrew Stuart. “The world is a big place.”

“It was once,” said Mr Fogg quietly.

“Once? Did the world get smaller?”

“Yes. Look at the newspaper. With the new railways and steamships, a man can go around the world in eighty days.”

Stuart laughed. “Eighty days, if everything goes well! But what about storms and accidents?”

“Eighty days, with everything included,” said Mr Fogg.

“Then I'll bet you four thousand pounds it's impossible!”

“It is quite possible. And I will bet twenty thousand pounds that I can do it. Who accepts?”

Twenty thousand pounds was half of everything Mr Fogg had. His friends accepted at once.

“There is a train to Dover at 8:45 tonight,” said Mr Fogg. “I will be on it. And I will be back in this room on Saturday 21 December, at 8:45 in the evening.”

“And what about the unexpected?” asked Stuart.

“The unexpected does not exist,” said Mr Fogg. Then he went back to his cards.

At ten to eight he came home — four hours early.

“We leave for Dover in ten minutes,” said Mr Fogg. “We are going around the world.”

Passepartout's mouth fell open. “Around the world?”

“In eighty days. No trunks. Just one bag. We'll buy clothes on the way.”

Mr Fogg put a thick packet of banknotes into the bag. “Twenty thousand pounds,” he said. “Take good care of it.”

At 8:45 exactly, the train left. Suddenly Passepartout gave a cry.

“Oh, sir! In my hurry I forgot to turn off the gas lamp in my room!”

“Then it will burn until we come back,” said Mr Fogg calmly. “At your expense. You will pay for the gas.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Detective
chapters.text:
Soon all London was talking about Phileas Fogg. The newspapers called him a madman. People bet money on him, like a horse in a race.

On 9 October, a small, thin man with sharp eyes was walking up and down the harbour at Suez, in Egypt. His name was Fix, and he was a detective. In his pocket he had a description of the bank thief: a tall, well-dressed English gentleman. Fix was waiting for the steamship Mongolia, which was coming from Europe on its way to India.

“The thief will try to run away to India or even further,” he thought. “And I'll be here when he arrives.”

The Mongolia arrived, and a cheerful young Frenchman came up to him with a passport.

“Excuse me, where can I get this stamped?”

Fix looked at the passport, and his heart jumped. Tall, well-dressed English gentleman — this was the man!

“The owner must come to the office himself,” said Fix.

Later, Fix met Passepartout again in the street, and the Frenchman was happy to talk.

“We left London a week ago, with only ten minutes to get ready,” said Passepartout. “No trunks, only one bag — with twenty thousand pounds in it! My master is going around the world in eighty days. It's a bet, he says.”

“A bet!” thought Fix. “What a story! He's the thief, I'm sure of it.” He hurried to send a telegram to London: “Bank thief found. Name: Phileas Fogg. Send warrant for his arrest to Bombay. — Fix.” A warrant was a special paper from a judge. Without it, he couldn't arrest anybody.

Then Fix got on the Mongolia too.

During the voyage, Mr Fogg played cards from morning to night. He never looked at the sea. Passepartout, on the other hand, enjoyed everything — the sun, the sea, the food, and his new friend, Mr Fix, who was always ready to buy him a drink.

On 20 October they arrived in Bombay — two days early. Mr Fogg wrote in his little notebook: “Two days gained.” Then he went to have dinner at the station before the train to Calcutta.

But in Bombay there was no warrant for Fix. “It isn't here yet!” he thought angrily. “And I can't stop him without it.”

Passepartout, meanwhile, was walking around the city with his mouth open. Snake charmers! Elephants! Dancers! Then he saw a beautiful temple on a hill, and he went inside to look. He didn't know that he had to take his shoes off first.

Suddenly three angry priests jumped on him. They threw him to the floor and pulled off his shoes. Passepartout fought back, jumped up and ran — without his shoes and without his hat. He arrived at the station just in time, in his socks.

“What happened to you?” asked Mr Fogg.

Passepartout told him the whole story, red in the face.

“I hope it won't happen again,” said Mr Fogg coldly, and he got on the train.

But Fix, who was hiding behind a column, heard everything. He smiled.

“A crime in India!” he thought. “Now I can stop him!”

The train left for Calcutta. But Fix did not get on it. He had a better idea.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Elephant
chapters.text:
On the train to Calcutta, Mr Fogg sat with Sir Francis Cromarty, an English general. They met on the Mongolia, and now they played cards together while India went past the windows: green hills, rivers, small villages and jungle.

On the morning of 22 October, the train suddenly stopped in the middle of the forest.

“Everybody off! Passengers get off here!” shouted a railwayman.

“Why?” asked Sir Francis. “Where are we?”

“At the village of Kholby, sir. The railway isn't finished. It starts again at Allahabad, fifty miles from here.”

“But the newspapers in London said that the railway was finished!” cried Sir Francis.

“The newspapers were wrong,” said Mr Fogg calmly. “It doesn't matter. I am two days early.”

The other passengers quickly took every cart and horse in the village. Nothing was left. Then Passepartout came back with an idea.

“Sir, I found an elephant!”

The elephant's name was Kiouni. His owner didn't want to sell him, so Mr Fogg offered more money, and then more — and in the end he paid two thousand pounds.

“Two thousand pounds for an elephant!” whispered Passepartout. He felt sick.

Mr Fogg also found a guide, a young man who knew the jungle. Sir Francis came with them too. The guide sat on the elephant's neck, and the three men sat on his back. Every time Kiouni took a step, Passepartout jumped up and down like a ball. He bit his tongue twice.

They travelled all day through the thick forest. On the second day, the guide stopped the elephant and listened. There was strange music in the distance — drums and bells and singing.

“Quick! Hide!” he whispered.

They hid among the trees and watched. A long line of people came along the path. First came priests in long robes. Behind them, men carried the body of a dead old man in rich clothes. He was a rajah — a prince. And behind him, among the priests, walked a young woman. She was very beautiful and very pale, and she walked slowly, like a person in a dream.

“Who is she?” asked Sir Francis quietly.

“The rajah's widow,” said the guide. “Her name is Aouda. She comes from a rich family in Bombay, and she went to an English school. But they made her marry this old rajah, and now he is dead. Tomorrow morning they will burn her on the fire with his body.”

“Burn her alive?” said Sir Francis. “And she doesn't want to?”

“Of course not. They gave her a drug — opium — so she doesn't understand what's happening.”

For a minute nobody spoke. Then Mr Fogg took out his watch and looked at it.

“I have twelve hours to spare,” he said. “I can use them to save that woman.”

Sir Francis looked at him in surprise. “Why, Mr Fogg, you have a heart after all!”

“Sometimes,” said Mr Fogg. “When I have the time.”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Aouda
chapters.text:
The priests took Aouda into an old temple for the night. Outside, men with swords walked up and down. Nearby stood a huge pile of wood, with the dead rajah on top.

Mr Fogg, Sir Francis and the guide waited in the dark. They tried to cut through the back wall of the temple, but the guards came, and they had to stop. Hours passed. Nobody had a plan. And where was Passepartout? Nobody saw him leave.

At dawn the crowd began to sing. The priests carried Aouda out of the temple and laid her on the wood next to her dead husband. Then they set fire to it.

Mr Fogg started to run forward. Sir Francis caught his arm. “Stop! They'll kill you!”

Suddenly a cry of terror went up from the crowd. On top of the fire, the dead rajah sat up! He stood up slowly in the smoke, took the young woman in his arms and walked down from the fire. The people fell on their faces. Nobody dared to look at him.

The rajah walked up to Mr Fogg. “Let's go!” he said.

It was Passepartout! During the night he climbed onto the pile of wood, put on the rajah's long robe and lay there, waiting.

They ran to the elephant. Behind them, bullets flew through the trees. But Kiouni was fast, and soon they were safe.

Aouda woke up at Allahabad, and the guide told her everything. Her eyes filled with tears, and she thanked them again and again. Mr Fogg said almost nothing.

“What will you do with the elephant now, sir?” asked Passepartout.

Mr Fogg turned to the guide. “You were a good guide and a brave man. Kiouni is yours.”

“What a present!” said Passepartout.

Aouda couldn't stay in India — the priests would find her. But she had a rich cousin in Hong Kong. So Mr Fogg decided to take her there.

At Allahabad they got on the train again, and they arrived in Calcutta on 25 October. At the station, a policeman stopped them.

“Mr Phileas Fogg? Come with me, please.”

In the courtroom sat the three priests from Bombay. On the table in front of the judge was a pair of shoes.

“My shoes!” cried Passepartout.

At the back of the room, Fix was hiding and smiling. The priests were his idea — he brought them to Calcutta himself.

The judge gave Passepartout fifteen days in prison, and Mr Fogg eight days. “A master must answer for his servant,” he said. Fix rubbed his hands. Eight days! Plenty of time for the warrant to arrive!

“Can I pay bail?” asked Mr Fogg. Bail was money that you paid to the court to go free for a while.

“Yes. A thousand pounds each.”

Mr Fogg put two thousand pounds on the table, and they walked out. At noon they were on a ship for Hong Kong.

“He throws money around like a thief!” said Fix furiously, and he followed them onto the ship.

There, on the deck, Passepartout saw him. “Mr Fix! You're going to Hong Kong too? What a coincidence!”

Passepartout began to think. Suez, Bombay, Hong Kong... Fix was always there. Then he understood — or he thought so.

“He's a spy!” he thought. “Those gentlemen from the club sent him to watch my master!”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Hong Kong
chapters.text:
There was bad weather all the way to Hong Kong, and the ship arrived one day late. That evening, Mr Fogg asked about Aouda's cousin. The news was bad: the cousin didn't live in Hong Kong any more. Two years before, he moved to Holland.

Aouda put her hands over her face.

“Then come with us to Europe,” said Mr Fogg, as if it was nothing. “Passepartout, book three cabins on the Carnatic for Yokohama.”

At the harbour, Passepartout learned some important news. The Carnatic was leaving that same evening, not the next morning.

Then Fix came up to him. The detective looked tired and worried. The warrant still wasn't there, and Hong Kong was the last British place on the journey. After this, there were no more British places until England — and he couldn't arrest Mr Fogg anywhere else.

“Come and have a drink,” said Fix. “I need to talk to you.”

They went into a dark little bar full of smoke. Fix ordered drinks. Then he put his hand on Passepartout's arm.

“I'm a detective,” he said quietly. “Your master is the man who robbed the Bank of England. Help me keep him in Hong Kong, and I'll give you five hundred pounds.”

Passepartout jumped to his feet. “My master? A thief? He's the most honest man in the world! You can keep your money, Mr Fix!”

He emptied his glass angrily, and Fix gave him another. Then someone put a pipe in his hand. It was opium. Passepartout smoked it, and the room began to turn round and round.

“I must tell my master... the ship... tonight...” he said. Then his head fell on the table.

Fix paid and walked out, smiling.

The next morning Mr Fogg and Aouda came to the harbour. The Carnatic was gone. And Passepartout was gone too.

Fix was waiting there. “Did you miss the ship too, sir?” he asked.

“Yes,” said Mr Fogg. Not a muscle moved in his face. He went to look for another boat.

He found a small, fast boat called the Tankadere. Its captain was John Bunsby.

“Yokohama is too far for my little boat,” said Bunsby. “But I can take you to Shanghai. The big American ship for San Francisco starts from there and stops at Yokohama on the way.”

“A hundred pounds a day,” said Mr Fogg, “and two hundred more if we arrive in time.”

Then he turned to Fix. “There is room for you too, sir, if you like.”

Fix's face went red. He was ashamed. But he accepted — he couldn't lose his man now.

The Tankadere flew over the water. Then a terrible storm came. Huge waves crashed over the little boat, and the wind screamed. Aouda was pale but brave. Mr Fogg stood on the deck in the rain as if he was at home in Savile Row.

On 11 November they were still a few miles from Shanghai when they saw black smoke. The American ship was leaving the harbour!

“Fire the gun!” said Mr Fogg.

Bunsby fired the little gun at the front of the boat — a signal for help. Boom! Boom!

On the big ship, a sailor looked through his telescope. And slowly, the ship began to turn towards them.

But where was Passepartout?

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Alone in Japan
chapters.text:
Passepartout woke up on the Carnatic, out at sea. His head was aching. How did he get here? Somehow, half asleep, he found his way from the bar to the ship in the night. Slowly he remembered everything — Fix, the pipe, the ship leaving that night.

“My master!” he cried. “He missed the ship, and it's my fault!”

He searched the ship from top to bottom. There was no Mr Fogg and no Aouda.

On 13 November the Carnatic arrived in Yokohama. Passepartout walked off the ship alone. He didn't speak a word of Japanese, and he had no money in his pockets. He felt very far from home.

He was hungry, so he sold his good European clothes and bought old Japanese ones. With the money that was left, he had a big meal.

“Now what?” he thought. Then he saw a big poster on a wall:

THE GREAT JAPANESE ACROBATS OF MR BATULCAR!
THE LONG NOSES!
LAST SHOW BEFORE THEIR TOUR OF AMERICA!

America! Passepartout ran straight to the circus.

“I was an acrobat in Paris,” he told Mr Batulcar. “I'm strong, and I can sing too.”

“You can be part of the human pyramid,” said Batulcar. “At the bottom.”

The Long Noses were famous. Each acrobat wore wings and a huge nose made of bamboo — two metres long! For the pyramid, the acrobats lay on their backs, with their noses pointing up at the sky. Other acrobats stood on their noses, and others stood on top of them, higher and higher.

That evening the theatre was full. The music played, and the pyramid went up and up. Passepartout lay at the bottom with five men on his nose.

Then he looked out at the audience — and he saw a calm English face in the front row.

“My master! My master!” he shouted.

He jumped up, and the whole pyramid came down — crash! — onto the stage. Acrobats and noses flew in all directions. Passepartout ran through the audience, still wearing his wings.

“Ah, there you are,” said Mr Fogg.

What happened? The American ship took Mr Fogg and Aouda to Yokohama. Mr Fogg spent the day looking for Passepartout everywhere, and in the evening he went to the circus — and found him.

Mr Fogg paid Batulcar for the damage, and they ran to the harbour. Half an hour later they were on the General Grant, on their way across the Pacific to San Francisco.

Passepartout didn't tell his master about Fix. He felt too ashamed. But one day, on the deck, he saw a small, thin man with sharp eyes.

It was Fix.

Passepartout didn't say a word. He hit Fix — hard — and then again. He felt much better.

Fix stood up slowly and touched his face.

“Finished?” he asked. “Good. Now listen. Before, I was your master's enemy. Now I'm on his side. My warrant came at last in Yokohama, but it only works on British land. So I want him to get to England as fast as possible. Then we'll see if he's a thief or not.”

Passepartout looked at him for a long time.

“The same side? Maybe,” he said. “Friends? Never. And if you try any more tricks, I'll break your neck.”

chapters.title: Chapter 7. America
chapters.text:
On 3 December the General Grant arrived in San Francisco. The train to New York didn't leave until the evening, so Mr Fogg and Aouda went for a walk.

The streets were full of people. There was an election, and two crowds were shouting at each other. Suddenly the shouting turned into a fight. Sticks flew through the air. A huge man with a red beard swung his fist at Mr Fogg. Fix jumped in front of him and took the blow on his own head.

“Yankee!” said Mr Fogg coldly.

“Englishman!” said the big man. “We'll meet again!”

“I hope so. Your name, sir?”

“Colonel Stamp W. Proctor.”

“Phileas Fogg.”

That evening the train left San Francisco. It was a long train, with sleeping cars and a restaurant car. They had seven days of travel in front of them — across deserts, mountains and great empty plains.

On the third day, the train stopped in the middle of the plain. In front of it, thousands and thousands of buffalo were crossing the railway. It was like a brown river with horns. Nobody could stop them, so the train waited. Three hours later, the last buffalo walked slowly across.

“What a country!” said Passepartout. “Here even cows can stop a train!”

Mr Fogg said nothing. He just played cards.

Then, near a place called Medicine Bow, the train stopped again. The driver came back with bad news.

“The bridge in front of us is old and badly damaged. It could fall at any moment.”

“So what can we do?” asked the passengers.

“Well,” said the driver, “if we go across very, very fast, maybe the bridge won't have time to fall.”

All the passengers liked this idea. Only Passepartout had a question.

“Wouldn't it be better if the passengers walked across first, and then the train came after them?”

But nobody listened to him. The driver went back to the engine. The train moved back a mile, then it went forward faster and faster and faster. It didn't run across the bridge — it almost flew across.

A second later, the bridge fell into the river with a terrible crash.

Two days later, Passepartout was walking along the train when he saw a big man with a red beard. Colonel Proctor! He ran to tell Fix. Fix and Aouda decided to keep Mr Fogg busy with cards, so that he wouldn't see the colonel.

But Proctor came into their car. He stood next to the card table and laughed loudly.

“You don't know how to play cards, Englishman!”

Mr Fogg stood up. “Sir, you and I have some business to finish.”

They decided to fight there and then, with pistols, in the last car of the train. The conductor agreed to keep the car empty.

The two men walked to the end of the train. Each of them had a pistol in his hand. Aouda was white with fear.

And then, outside, came wild cries and the sound of shooting. Men on horses were galloping beside the train.

It was the Sioux.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Over the Snow
chapters.text:
Dozens of Sioux warriors jumped from their horses onto the moving train. They ran along the roofs of the cars. Some climbed into the engine.

Mr Fogg and Colonel Proctor forgot their fight at once. They shot from the windows side by side. Aouda fought bravely too, with a pistol in her hand. Passengers shouted, glass broke, and the train raced on faster and faster, because the Sioux hit the driver on the head, and now nobody was driving it.

“We must stop the train!” shouted the conductor. “Fort Kearney is just two miles away. There are soldiers there. If we go past the fort, we are all dead!”

“I'll stop it,” said Passepartout.

He opened a door, slipped down under the train and crawled forward along the chains between the cars. The wheels were roaring next to his head. At last he reached the place where the engine was joined to the train. He pulled with all his strength, and the iron hook came open.

The engine raced away alone. The cars slowed down and stopped — just a few hundred metres from Fort Kearney.

Soldiers ran out of the fort. The Sioux turned their horses and rode away.

But when they counted the passengers, three men were missing. One of them was Passepartout. The Sioux took them away as prisoners.

Mr Fogg looked at Aouda. Then he turned to the captain of the soldiers.

“I'm going to find my servant. Alive or dead.”

“Sir, it's very dangerous,” said the captain. “But thirty of my men will go with you.”

Mr Fogg knew what this meant. If he went, he could lose the bet. Still, he went.

Aouda stayed at the fort with Fix. She thought about this cold, quiet Englishman, who never showed his feelings. He was risking everything for his servant. She was beginning to love him.

The night was long and freezing. It began to snow. In the morning there were shots in the distance. Then the soldiers came back — with Passepartout and the two other men. Everybody cheered.

But the train was gone. The driver brought the engine back, and the train left during the night without them. They were now twenty hours late.

“I know a way,” said Fix. He was on Mr Fogg's side now. “There's a man here called Mudge. He has a sledge with a sail. It flies over the snow like a boat over water.”

Mr Fogg paid Mudge, and they set off across the white plains. The wind filled the sail, and the sledge flew. Aouda sat wrapped in furs. Behind them, a pack of hungry wolves ran for miles. Passepartout watched them nervously.

In the evening they reached Omaha and caught a train to Chicago, and from there another train to New York.

At a quarter past eleven at night on 11 December, they ran onto the dock in New York. The ship for Liverpool was called the China.

It was gone.

It left at half past ten — just forty-five minutes before they arrived.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The Henrietta
chapters.text:
Mr Fogg did not get angry. He did not say a word. He just went to a hotel and slept.

Early the next morning he walked along the river, looking for a ship. At last he found one with smoke coming out of its chimney. It was called the Henrietta. Its captain, Andrew Speedy, was a small, angry man with a voice like a dog barking.

“I need to go to Liverpool,” said Mr Fogg.

“Liverpool? No! I'm going to Bordeaux, in France. And I don't take passengers.”

“I will pay you two thousand dollars a person to Bordeaux,” said Mr Fogg.

The captain stopped barking. “Well... for that money... all right.”

At nine o'clock the Henrietta left New York.

The next day, a strange thing happened. Captain Speedy was locked in his cabin, shouting and kicking the door. And Mr Fogg was steering the ship — towards Liverpool. How? He paid the sailors well, and they were happy to help him.

They had a fast journey, in spite of the storms. But on the fourth day, the engineer came to Mr Fogg.

“Sir, the coal is nearly finished. We won't have enough for Liverpool.”

“Then let Captain Speedy out,” said Mr Fogg.

The captain came out like a bomb. “Thief! Pirate! I'll—”

“Captain,” said Mr Fogg, “I want to buy your ship.”

“My ship? Never!”

“Sixty thousand dollars.”

The captain was silent. The Henrietta was old. It wasn't worth half that money.

“And I can keep the bottom of the ship, and the engine?” he asked.

“Yes. I only need the wood.”

“Then it's yours!”

And Mr Fogg began to burn his ship. First the cabins went into the fire, then the beds, then the masts, then the deck. Every hour the Henrietta got smaller. Captain Speedy watched and cried, “Oh, my poor ship!” — but he held his sixty thousand dollars tightly.

On 20 December they reached Ireland. They took a train across Ireland, then a fast boat across the sea. At 11:40 in the morning on 21 December, Mr Fogg stepped onto the dock at Liverpool.

London was only six hours away by train. He had nine hours. He was going to win!

Then a hand touched his shoulder.

“Phileas Fogg,” said Fix, “I arrest you in the name of the Queen!”

Mr Fogg sat in a small prison cell. He put his watch on the table in front of him and watched the minutes go by. One o'clock. Two o'clock. Half past two.

At 2:33 there was a noise in the corridor. The door opened. Fix ran in, out of breath, with his hair everywhere.

“Sir... I'm sorry... a terrible mistake... The police caught the real thief three days ago. You are free!”

Mr Fogg looked at the detective. Then, for the first and only time in his life, he moved fast. He hit Fix, and Fix fell on the floor.

“Well done, sir!” cried Passepartout.

Mr Fogg ordered a special train. It raced towards London through the snow.

But they arrived at 8:50 in the evening. Five minutes too late.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. The Lost Day
chapters.text:
Mr Fogg went home to Savile Row. He was ruined. The journey took almost all his money, and now the twenty thousand pounds belonged to his friends at the club.

In Passepartout's room, the gas lamp was still burning — day and night, for eighty days, at his expense. Passepartout turned it off with a heavy heart. “It's my fault,” he thought. “Why did I go into that bar in Hong Kong?”

The next day Mr Fogg did not go to the club. He stayed in his room. In the evening he asked to speak to Aouda.

“Madam,” he said, “I brought you to England. I wanted to make your life comfortable here. But now I am a poor man, and I cannot. I am very sorry.”

Aouda stood up and took his hand.

“Mr Fogg,” she said, “I don't need money. But you need a friend now. Will you have me — as your wife?”

Mr Fogg's eyes shone, and for a moment his lips shook a little.

“I love you,” he said simply. “Yes. I am yours.”

They called Passepartout. His face lit up like the sun. “I'll go to Reverend Wilson at once,” he said. “Is the wedding tomorrow, Monday?”

“Yes, tomorrow, Monday,” said Aouda.

It was five past eight. Passepartout hurried off.

At 8:35 he ran back into the house. His hair was wild, his hat was gone, and he could hardly breathe.

“Sir... the wedding... impossible... tomorrow!”

“Why?”

“Because tomorrow is Sunday!”

“No. Tomorrow is Monday.”

“No! Today is Saturday! Saturday the twenty-first! We made a mistake of one day! But you have only ten minutes!”

Passepartout pushed his master out of the door and into a cab.

What happened? When you travel east, you travel towards the sun. So every day of your journey is a few minutes shorter. All the way around the world, those minutes add up to one whole day. So Mr Fogg counted eighty days, but in London only seventy-nine days passed.

At the Reform Club, his five friends were sitting nervously under the big clock.

“8:40,” said Andrew Stuart. “Five more minutes and we win.”

“8:43... 8:44...”

Fifty-seven seconds... fifty-eight... fifty-nine... And the door opened.

“Here I am, gentlemen,” said Phileas Fogg.

He won the twenty thousand pounds. But the journey cost him almost nineteen thousand. He gave the money that was left to Passepartout and Fix. (He didn't feel angry with Fix any more.) But from Passepartout's share he took the cost of the gas — one thousand nine hundred and twenty hours of it.

On Monday, Phileas Fogg and Aouda were married. Passepartout stood next to them, as happy as a child.

So what did Mr Fogg gain from his journey around the world? Nothing, you might say. Only a beautiful, brave wife, who made him the happiest man in England.

Wouldn't you go around the world for less?
